source_text: Quibus duobus dominis neget posse seruiri, quia alterum offendi sit necesse alterum defendi, ipse declarat, deum proponens et mamonam. proinde mamonam quem intellegi uelit, si interpretem non habes, ab ipso potes discere. admonens enim nos de saecularibus suffragia nobis prospicere amicitiarum secundum serui illius exemplum, qui ab actu summotus dominicos debitores diminutis cautionibus releuat in subsidium sibi: et ego, inquit, dico uobis, facite uobis amicos de mamona iniustitiae, de nummo scilicet, de ' quo et seruus ille. iniustitiae enim auctorem et dominatorem totius saeculi nummum scimus omnes. cui famulatam uidens Pharisaeorum cupiditatem ammentauit hanc sententiam: non potestis deo seruire et mamonae. inridebant denique Pharisaei pecuniae cupidi, quod intellexissent scilicet mamonam de nummo dictum, ne quia existimet in mamona creatorem intellegendum et Christum a creatoris illos seruitute reuocasse.. quid nunc? potius ex hoc disce unum a Christo deum ostensum. duos enim dominos nominauit, deum et mamonam, crea. torem et nummum: denique non potestis deo seruire, utique ei, cui uidebantur seruire, et mamonam, cui magis destinabantur. quodsi ipse alium se ageret, non duos dominos, sed tres demonstrasset — et creator enim dominus, quia deus, et utique magis dominus quam mamonas magisque homini obseruandus, qua magis dominus —; quale est enim, ut qui mamonam dominum dixerat et cum domino iunxerat uero, ipsum dominum taceret, id est deum creatorem? aut numquid tacendo eo concessit seruiendum ei esse, si solummodo sibi et mamonae negauit posse seruiri? ita cum unum deum ponit, nominaturus et creatorem, si alius esset ipse, creatorem nominauit quem [dominum] sine alio [deo non] posuit. et illud itaque relucebit, quomodo dictum sit: (si) in mamona iniusto fideles non extitistis, quod uerum est quis uobis credet? in nummo scilicet iniusto, non in creatore, quem et Marcion iustum facit, et: si in alieno fideles inuenti non estis, meum quis dabit uobis? alienum enim debet esse a semis dei quod iniustum est. creator autem quomodo alienus erat Pharisaeis, proprius deus Iudaicae gentis? si ergo haec non cadunt in creatorem, sed in mamonam, 'quis uobis credet quod uerius est'? et 'quis uobis dabit quod meum est'? non potest quasi ali{en)us dixisse de alterius dei gratia. tunc enim uideretur ita dixisse, si eos in creatorem, non in mamonam infideles notando per creatoris mentionem distinctione se fecisset dei alterius, non commissuri suam ueritatem infidelibus creatoris, t quoniam tunc alterius uideri potest, si non ad hoc proponatur, ut a re, de qua agitur, separetur. Si autem et iustificantes se coram hominibus Pharisaei spem mercedis in homine ponebant, illo eos sensu increpabat, quo et propheta Hieremias: miser homo, qui spem habet in homine. si et adicit: scit autem deus corda uestra, illius dei uim commemorabat, (qui) lucernam se pronuntiarat scrutantem renes et corda. si superbiam tangit: quod elatum est apud homines perosum est deo, Esaiam ponit ante oculos: dies enim domini Sabaoth in omnem contumeliosum et superbum, in omnem sublimem et elatum, et humiliabuntur. Possum iam colligere, cur tanto aeuo deus Marcionis fuerit in occulto. expectabat, opinor, donec haec omnia disceret a creatore. didicit igitur usque ad Iohannis tempora atque ita exinde processit adnuntiare regnum dei dicens: lex et prophetae usque ad Iohannem; ex quo regnum dei adnuntiatur. quasi non et nos limitem quendam agnoscamus Iohannem constitutum inter uetera et noua, ad quem desineret Iudaismus et a quo inciperet Christianismus, non tamen, ut ab alia uirtute facta sit sedatio legis et prophetarum et initiatio euangelii, in quo est dei regnum.' [Christus ipse.] nam id si probauimus, et uetera transitura et noua successura praedicari a creatore, si et Iohannes antecursor et praeparator ostenditur uiarum domini euangelium', superducturi et regnum dei promulgaturi, et ex hoc iam, quod Iohannes uenit, ipse erit Christus qui Iohannem erit subsecutus ut antecursorem; et, si desierunt uetera et coeperunt ! noua interstite Iohanne, non erit mirum quod ex dispositione est creatoris, ut unde(unde) magis probetur ** quam ex legis et prophetarum in Iohannem occasu et exinde ortu regni dei. transeat igitur caelum et terra citius, sicut et lex et: prophetae, quam unus apexuerborum domini-nerbum enim, inquit Esaias, dei nostri manet in aeuum —: nam quoniam in Esaia iam tunc Christus, sermo scilicet et spiritus creatoris, Iohannem praedicarat — uocem clamantis in deserto: parate uiam domini — in hoc uenturum, ut legis et] prophetarum ordo exinde cessaret, per adimpletionem, non per destructionem, et regnum dei a Christo adnuntiaretur, I ideo subtexuit facilius elementa transitura quam uerba sua,' confirmans hoc quoque, quod de Iohanne dixerat, non praeterisse.
pass_a_gloss: To whom he denies that it is possible to serve two lords, because it is necessary to offend one and defend the other, he himself declares, proposing God and mammon. Therefore, mammon, which he wants to be understood, if you do not have an interpreter, you can learn from him. For, warning us to look out for worldly friendships according to the example of that servant, who, removed from action, relieves the debtors of his lord by diminishing their securities for his own benefit: and I, he says, tell you, make friends for yourselves from mammon of injustice, from money, of course, from which also that servant. For we know that money is the author and ruler of all the world's injustice. Seeing the greed of the Pharisees serving this, he strengthened this sentence: you cannot serve God and mammon. Finally, the Pharisees, greedy for money, were ridiculing, because they had understood, of course, that mammon was said about money, lest they think that the creator is to be understood in mammon and that Christ recalled them from the service of that creator. What now? Rather, learn from this that Christ shows one God. For he named two lords, God and mammon, the creator and money: finally, you cannot serve God, certainly to him, whom they seemed to serve, and mammon, to whom they were more devoted. But if he himself were acting as another, he would have shown not two lords, but three — and the creator is indeed the lord, because he is God, and certainly a greater lord than mammon, and more to be obeyed by man, because he is a greater lord —; what kind of thing is it, that he who said mammon is lord and joined it with the true lord, would be silent about the true lord himself, that is, the creator God? Or did he, by being silent about him, concede that he should be served, if only he denied that it is possible to serve him and mammon? Thus, when he sets forth one God, naming also the creator, if he himself were another, he named the creator, whom he set forth as lord without another God. And that will also become clear, how it was said: if you have not been faithful in mammon of injustice, what is true, who will trust you? Certainly in unjust money, not in the creator, whom Marcion also makes just, and: if you have not been found faithful in what is another's, who will give you what is mine? For what is another's must be alien to the semi-god, which is unjust. But how was the creator alien to the Pharisees, the proper God of the Jewish nation? If, therefore, these things do not fall to the creator, but to mammon, who will trust you with what is truer? And who will give you what is mine? He cannot have said this as if it were another's, by the grace of another god. For then he would seem to have said this, if he had noted them as unfaithful in the creator, not in mammon, by mentioning the creator, making a distinction of another god, not entrusting his truth to the unfaithful of the creator. But if the Pharisees, justifying themselves before men, were putting their hope of reward in men, he was rebuking them with the sense in which also the prophet Jeremiah: woe to the man who puts his hope in man. And if he adds: but God knows your hearts, he was commemorating the power of that God, who had declared himself to be the searcher of kidneys and hearts. If he touches on pride: what is exalted among men is an abomination to God, he sets Isaiah before their eyes: for the day of the Lord of hosts will be upon every arrogant and haughty one, and upon every lofty and exalted one, and they will be humbled. For it is written, the day of the Lord of hosts in every contemptuous and proud, in every lofty and exalted, and they will be humbled, as Isaiah says. Now I can gather why the God of Marcion was in hiding for so long. He was waiting, I think, until he learned all these things from the creator. Therefore, he learned up to the time of John and thus proceeded to announce the kingdom of God, saying: the law and the prophets were until John; from whom the kingdom of God is announced. As if we do not recognize a certain boundary established by John between the old and the new, at which Judaism ceases and Christianity begins, not, however, that the cessation of the law and the prophets and the initiation of the gospel, in which is the kingdom of God, was made by another virtue. For if we have proven this, that the old things are passing away and the new things are succeeding, predicted by the creator, and John is shown to be the forerunner and preparer of the ways of the Lord, the gospel, which will bring and proclaim the kingdom of God, and from this, now that John has come, he himself will be Christ, who will follow John as a forerunner; and if the old things have ceased and the new things have begun, with John in between, it will not be surprising that this is from the disposition of the creator, so that it may be proven more than from the passing away of the law and the prophets in John and from the rising of the kingdom of God. Therefore, let heaven and earth pass away more quickly, just as also the law and the prophets, than one dot of the words of the Lord — for the word of the Lord, he says, remains forever —; for since in Isaiah, Christ, namely the word and spirit of the creator, had already predicted John, saying: a voice crying in the desert: prepare the way of the Lord, he was coming to this, that the order of the law and the prophets would cease from then on, through fulfillment, not destruction, and the kingdom of God would be announced by Christ. Therefore, he subjoined that the elements would pass away more easily than his words, confirming also what he had said about John, that he had not passed away.

choices.why: The Latin word 'mamona' refers to wealth or riches, as opposed to God.
The Latin word 'deus' refers to God, the creator of the universe.
The Latin word 'nummum' refers to money, as opposed to the creator or God.
The Latin word 'Iohannem' refers to John, the forerunner of Christ.
The Latin phrase 'regnum dei' refers to the kingdom of God, as announced by Christ.

pass_b_english: When Christ says you can't serve two masters, he's talking about God and money - what he calls 'mammon'. If you're not sure what he means by mammon, you can figure it out from his own words. He's warning us to be smart about our relationships with people, just like a servant who gets ahead by being kind to his master's debtors. Christ says, 'Make friends for yourselves by means of the mammon of unrighteousness' (Luke 16:9), which is just a fancy way of saying 'use your money to make friends'. We all know that money is the root of all kinds of evil, and the Pharisees were so greedy for it that they were basically serving money instead of God. That's why Christ says, 'You cannot serve God and money' (Luke 16:13). The Pharisees were ridiculing him, thinking he was just talking about money, but Christ was making a point about the dangers of loving money more than God. So what's the takeaway? Christ is showing us that there's only one God, and we can't serve both God and money. If he were talking about some other god, he would have said so, but instead he's clear that there's only one Lord - and that's the creator of the universe, not just some abstract idea of a god. If Christ were some other god, he would have said so, but instead he's saying that the creator is the one true God, and we can't serve both him and money. The Pharisees were so focused on their own wealth and status that they were putting their hope in the wrong things, and Christ is calling them out on it. As the prophet Jeremiah says, 'Woe to those who put their trust in human beings' (Jeremiah 17:5), and Christ is saying the same thing - don't put your hope in people or money, because God knows what's really in your heart. If you're not faithful with the money you have, how can you expect to be trusted with true riches? And if you're not faithful with what belongs to someone else, how can you expect to be given what's truly yours? The creator is not some distant, alien god - he's the God of the Jewish people, and he's the one who deserves our loyalty. So when Christ says we can't serve both God and money, he's not talking about some other god - he's talking about the one true God, the creator of the universe. The Pharisees were trying to justify themselves before men, but Christ is saying that's not enough - we need to be faithful to God, not just to people. And as Isaiah says, 'The day of the Lord of hosts will come, and every arrogant and haughty person will be humbled' (Isaiah 2:12). Now we can see why Marcion's god was hiding for so long - he was waiting for Christ to come and show us the truth. But Christ has come, and he's shown us that the law and the prophets were just the beginning - now it's time for the kingdom of God to be announced. John the Baptist was the boundary between the old and the new, and now that he's come, Christ is following close behind. The old ways are passing away, and the new ways are beginning - and it's all part of God's plan. So let heaven and earth pass away, but the words of the Lord will remain forever (Isaiah 40:8), because Christ is the word and spirit of the creator, and he's the one who's bringing the kingdom of God to us.
notes: The translation of 'dies enim domini Sabaoth in omnem contumeliosum et superbum, in omnem sublimem et elatum, et humiliabuntur' is attributed to Isaiah 2:17, not Isaiah 2:12.

review.notes: Pass B fails on multiple scripture citations and content accuracy. 1. Pass B cites 'Luke 16:9' and 'Luke 16:13' for the quotes 'Make friends for yourselves by means of the mammon of unrighteousness' and 'You cannot serve God and money'. While these are the biblical sources, the Locked Latin text does not contain these citations, and Pass A (the faithful translation) also does not include them. Pass B adds these citations as if they are in the source. 2. Pass B cites 'Isaiah 2:12' for 'The day of the Lord of hosts will come, and every arrogant and haughty person will be humbled', whereas the Latin text refers to Isaiah (the content matches Isaiah 2:17) and the reviewer note correctly identifies the discrepancy. 3. Pass B cites 'Isaiah 40:8' for 'the words of the Lord will remain forever', which is a correct identification of the verse, but Pass B adds significant interpretive filler not present in the Latin (e.g., 'it's all part of God's plan', 'now it's time for the kingdom of God to be announced'). 4. Pass B introduces a significant theological error/repetition not in the Latin: 'If Christ were some other god, he would have said so, but instead he's saying that the creator is the one true God...'. The Latin text is discussing the distinction between the creator and mammon/money, not the ontological nature of Christ as a god.
reasons: Pass B adds scripture citations (Luke 16:9, Luke 16:13) not present in the Locked Latin.
Pass B provides a paraphrase with significant interpretive additions ('it's all part of God's plan', 'now it's time for the kingdom of God to be announced') rather than a translation.
Pass B contains a false scripture citation for the Isaiah passage (Isaiah 2:12 instead of the implied Isaiah 2:17).
